home.h1: Run a great PTA year without drowning in school messages
home.lead: Fundraiser playbooks, volunteer templates, and simple ways to cut school-app noise down to what matters.

faq.q: What's the easiest PTA fundraiser?
faq.a: A restaurant spirit night: a local restaurant donates a share of one evening's sales, and volunteers mostly just promote it.

faq.q: How do I get fewer school notifications?
faq.a: Pick one channel per app, switch general posts to a digest where the app offers it, and keep instant alerts only for direct and urgent messages.

faq.q: Is PTA Playbook free?
faq.a: Yes. Guides and templates are free. Premium template kits may come later.

pages.label: App guide
pages.title: How to cut ParentSquare notifications down to what matters
pages.summary: ParentSquare lets you set Posts to Instant or Digest per school, while urgent alerts and critical notices stay on. Use digest for everyday posts so you aren't interrupted all day.

p: Tip: set one family email that both parents read, and put notification preference order on that address.

ParentSquare help (district help desk mirror): Instant delivers posts as soon as possible; Digest delivers in the evening in the school's time zone; Off skips non-urgent post notifications. Urgent Alerts & Notices (attendance, urgent alerts, critical auto notices) stay enabled: https://gcasda.help/support/solutions/articles/48001243631-manage-parentsquare-notification-settings
Account settings overview: https://parentsquare1736363850.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/39029028719117-Account-Settings-Overview

steps: On the web: from Home, click your name → Manage Account → Notification Settings. On the app: menu (≡) → Account → Notifications.
Under Posts, turn on the channels you want (app, email, and/or text where offered), then choose Digest for everyday posts instead of Instant.
Keep Urgent Alerts & Notices available — those critical notices cannot be fully turned off, and Off for posts is still overridden for urgent alerts.
Under Direct Messages, keep instant delivery on the channel you actually read (often app or email) so teacher DMs aren't buried.
If you have several schools or children, repeat per school/district row.
If you have multiple emails or phones on the account, set preferred contact order so digests go to the family inbox you both check.

pages.label: Guide
pages.title: Build one family school inbox in 20 minutes
pages.summary: Create one email address just for school, register it everywhere, filter it, share it with your co-parent, and review it weekly.
steps: Create a free email address just for school (for example, lastname.school@…).
Register it in every school app and give it to each teacher.
In your main email, add a filter for school domains with the label “School”.
Share the inbox with your co-parent.
Every Sunday, scan it, add dates to the family calendar, and archive.
Anything with a deadline gets a calendar event with a two-day reminder.

pages.label: Fundraiser playbook
pages.title: School fun run playbook
pages.summary: An eight-week plan for a school fun run: approvals, roles, pledges, safety, day-of logistics and follow-up.

p: Money handling: use a two-person count for any cash, and follow your PTA's financial procedures.

steps: 8 weeks out: get principal or district approval, pick a date and rain date, and choose a pledge platform.
6 weeks: recruit a lead and four committee roles (pledges, course and safety, volunteers, prizes and comms).
4 weeks: launch the pledge page, send the family letter, and open volunteer sign-up.
2 weeks: confirm the course, water, first aid and volunteer schedule.
Week of: send daily progress updates and post a class leaderboard.
Day of: run a check-in table, track laps per class, and photograph only kids with media consent.
After: send thank-yous within 48 hours, collect pledges within two weeks, and publish totals.

pages.label: Fundraiser playbook
pages.title: Restaurant spirit night playbook
pages.summary: The lowest-effort fundraiser: a local restaurant donates a share of one evening's sales.
steps: Ask restaurants that already run giveback nights (many chains have an online request form).
Confirm the percentage and whether flyers or mentions at checkout are required.
Schedule it mid-week.
Promote it one week before, one day before, and on the day.
Thank the restaurant publicly.
Get the sales report and payment date in writing.

pages.label: Fundraiser playbook
pages.title: Online spirit-wear store playbook (print-on-demand)
pages.summary: Sell school spirit wear through a print-on-demand store so you take orders online without holding inventory or sizing guesses in a closet.

p: Online spirit-wear / print-on-demand stores show up repeatedly in PTA fundraiser idea lists (for example https://www.apexleadershipco.com/resources/school-fundraiser-ideas and https://scanraise.com/blog/pta-fundraising-ideas).

steps: Get board/principal approval for logo use and any required vendor paperwork.
Pick a print-on-demand vendor that handles storefront, printing and shipping (compare fees, minimums and sample quality).
Approve 3–6 designs (keep kid photos and last names off public product images).
Set the school cut of each item and a clear order window (for example 2–3 weeks).
Launch the store link via ParentSquare/email and classroom shares; pin sizing charts.
Promote once at launch, once mid-window, and once in the final 48 hours.
After the window closes, confirm fulfillment timelines with the vendor and thank families when tracking goes out.
Report net proceeds to the treasurer with the vendor payout statement.

pages.label: Fundraiser playbook
pages.title: School book fair volunteer and logistics playbook
pages.summary: A book fair runs on early volunteer recruiting, clear shift roles, cash/card handling, and a media-consent rule so kids aren't named or tagged in promo photos.

p: Book-fair organizing guides stress recruiting volunteers well ahead of the fair week (often starting about 6–8 weeks out): https://www.volunteerbadge.com/blog/school-book-fair-organizing-guide
Book fairs also appear as staple school events in broader PTA fundraiser roundups such as https://www.apexleadershipco.com/resources/school-fundraiser-ideas

steps: Confirm dates, vendor (for example Scholastic) and whether the fair is in-person, online or both with the school office.
About 6–8 weeks out: recruit a chair plus shift leads; use specific role asks (cashier, floater, setup, teardown) rather than a vague 'help needed' blast.
Build a SignUpGenius (or similar) with short shifts and a short how-to for each role.
Week before: confirm cash box / card reader, wishlist for classrooms/teachers, and preview night if you offer one.
During the fair: one person owns cash reconciliation each shift; keep student helpers off cash drawers.
Media rule: no kids' full names or tagged faces on public PTA posts unless you have current media consent on file — prefer product shots, tables and posters.
After: thank volunteers within a week, report proceeds, and note what to change next year.
pages.flag: General guidance — follow your school's vendor contract and media-consent policy.

pages.label: Fundraiser playbook
pages.title: Giving Tuesday playbook for a PTA or PTO
pages.summary: Giving Tuesday falls on December 1, 2026, the Tuesday after Thanksgiving. A simple one-day online ask with a clear goal, a matching gift if you can get one, and three reminder messages is enough for most PTAs.
steps: T-6 weeks: get board and principal approval, and confirm your PTA's nonprofit/tax status and how donations are receipted.
T-5 weeks: pick one concrete goal (for example, classroom libraries) and a dollar target.
T-4 weeks: ask a local business or family for a matching gift.
T-2 weeks: set up the donation page on the platform your PTA already uses, and test a $1 donation.
T-1 week: announce in the newsletter; schedule reminders for the morning, lunchtime and evening of Dec 1.
Day-of: post progress updates toward the goal.
Within 48 hours: thank every donor and share the total.

ul: Follow your PTA's bylaws and treasurer procedures; two people should reconcile online donations against the platform report.
Check your state PTA guidance and school district rules before naming a business sponsor.

pages.label: Guide
pages.title: Parent-teacher conference prep: a 15-minute checklist
pages.summary: Before the meeting, look at recent grades and work, ask your child what's going well and what's hard, and write down your top three questions in order. In the meeting, share what you see at home, take notes, and agree on one next step and how you'll stay in touch.
steps: A few days before: review recent grades, homework, tests and teacher messages in your school's portal or app.
Ask your child: How do you feel about school? What do you do well? What do you wish you had more help with?

Write your questions in order of importance, since slots are short. Good ones: Is my child meeting grade-level expectations? Can I see work where they did well and where they struggled? How are they doing socially? What can I do at home?
Note anything the teacher should know: interests, health issues, changes at home.
If you need an interpreter, ask the school ahead of time.
During: take notes, ask what terms or acronyms mean, and ask the best way to contact the teacher.
Before you leave: summarize the next steps out loud so you both agree.
After: send a short thank-you with any question you ran out of time for, and put follow-up dates on the family calendar.

p: Ask how the school measures progress, what support or services are available, and whether to set a check-in date. A conference is different from an IEP meeting; ask the school how to request an evaluation if you think your child needs one.

pages.label: Community drive playbook
pages.title: Holiday food drive playbook for a PTA or PTO
pages.summary: Partner with your local food bank first and ask what they need most, then run a short, two-week drive with a clear list, labeled bins, a class challenge if your principal approves, and a drop-off plan agreed with the food bank.
steps: T-5 weeks: get board and principal approval, and check district rules on collections and class competitions.
Find your local food bank with Feeding America's locator and ask what items they need, what they can't accept (often glass, opened or expired items), and how they want donations delivered.
T-3 weeks: set dates (two weeks is plenty), recruit 4–6 volunteers, and get boxes or bins labeled by item type.
T-2 weeks: announce with the food bank's most-needed list in the newsletter and school app; post one reminder a week.
During the drive: empty bins daily, check dates, and store items somewhere the custodian agrees to.
Delivery: drop off on the schedule the food bank gave you and get a receipt or weight total.
After: share the total and thank families, staff and the food bank.

ul: Optional: let families donate money directly to the food bank through its own website instead of collecting cash at school.
If you run a class challenge, keep the prize small and non-food (for example, extra recess, with the principal's OK).
Don't ask students to identify families who need help; privacy comes first.

p: Feeding America: Find your local food bank — https://www.feedingamerica.org/find-your-local-foodbank

pages.label: Community drive playbook
pages.title: Winter coat and clothing drive playbook for a PTA or PTO
pages.summary: Partner with a local nonprofit first and ask what sizes and items they need, then run a short fall/winter collection with labeled bins, clean wearable coats only, scheduled pickups, and a thank-you that shares the total.
steps: T-6 weeks: get board and principal approval. Confirm district rules on on-campus collections and any student competitions.

Find a distribution partner before you place bins. Options include a local shelter, school counselor network, or a registered One Warm Coat drive that connects you to their Nonprofit Network. Ask which sizes are scarce, whether hats/gloves/scarves are wanted, and how/when they accept deliveries.
T-4 weeks: set a clear one-sentence goal and a short window (about 2–4 weeks). Recruit a coordinator, 2–3 bin checkers, and a delivery driver. Line up dry indoor storage the custodian approves.
T-2 weeks: announce in the newsletter and school app with the partner's wish list (clean, wearable coats; note what not to donate). Place labeled bins in high-traffic spots the office agrees to.
During the drive: empty bins on a fixed schedule, reject damaged or unsanitary items, and keep coats dry. Sort by size before delivery if your partner wants that.
Delivery: contact the partner, drop off on their schedule, and get a count or receipt. Recycle truly unwearable coats through a textile recycler rather than dumping them.
After: share the total with families, thank volunteers and the partner, and note what to change next year.

ul: Optional: list your drive on One Warm Coat's public map if you want community drop-offs beyond the school (up to their site limit per registration).
Don't ask students to identify families who need coats; privacy comes first. Let the partner handle distribution.
If you run a class challenge, keep prizes small and non-clothing (for example extra recess) with the principal's OK.
New coats are great when budgets allow; gently used clean coats are the usual ask.

p: One Warm Coat: Organizer Guide — https://www.onewarmcoat.org/organizer-resources/plan/organizer-guide/

pages.title: Teacher Appreciation Week planning checklist for a PTA or PTO
pages.summary: Confirm the current year's National PTA and NEA dates early, form a small committee with a budget, ask staff how they prefer to be thanked, then run a simple one-idea-per-day week with thank-you notes, certificates and #ThankATeacher posts—no obligatory gift spend for families.
steps: Confirm dates for the upcoming Teacher Appreciation Week on National PTA and NEA (dates shift by year). Put the week on the PTA calendar 3–4 months ahead.
Form a 3–5 person committee and set a budget the board approves. Decide what is PTA-funded vs optional classroom gifts so families never feel pressured to spend.

Ask teachers and staff (anonymous short form) what they actually want: notes from students, coffee/snack cart, duty coverage, supply restock, or quiet work time. Skip scented candles if allergies are a concern.
Download National PTA's free Celebration Toolkit (thank-you cards, certificates, flyers, coloring pages, social graphics) and adapt to your school colors.

Draft a one-activity-per-day plan (for example: student notes Monday, staff breakfast Tuesday, certificates Wednesday, student art Thursday, principal shout-outs Friday). Recruit volunteers with SignUpGenius or your school tool.
Message families two weeks out: how to participate, that gifts are optional, and where to drop notes. Coordinate with the principal so classroom time is protected.
During the week: post once a day with #ThankATeacher if your PTA uses social, and include specialists, aides, custodians and office staff—not only homeroom teachers.
After: send a short thank-you to volunteers, note what worked in the board folder, and capture ideas for next year.

ul: Student and family handwritten notes beat pricey gifts for many teachers.
Use National PTA certificates signed by the principal or PTA president.
Partner with a local coffee shop for a donated drink cart if your district allows it.
Offer 15-minute duty coverage so teachers can take a real break.

p: National PTA: Teacher Appreciation Week — https://www.pta.org/home/events/PTA-Teacher-Appreciation-Week
NEA: Teacher Appreciation Week — https://www.nea.org/TAW

faq.q: When is Teacher Appreciation Week?
faq.a: Dates change each year. As of this page's research, NEA listed May 4–8, 2026 (National Teacher Appreciation Day May 5), and National PTA listed May 2–8, 2027 for its next featured week. Always confirm the current year on National PTA and NEA before you print flyers.

faq.q: Do families have to buy gifts?
faq.a: No. Plan so appreciation works even if families only write a note. Say clearly that gifts are optional and that the PTA is covering building-wide thanks.

pages.title: December school-parent checklist
pages.summary: December is short and busy: lock in winter break and early-release dates, make sure you will actually get snow-day and closure alerts, wrap up holiday drives and teacher thank-yous without pressure to spend, and send kids out dressed for the cold.
steps: Put winter break, early-release days and the first day back on the family calendar from the district's official calendar, not a flyer.

Check that closure and delay alerts reach you: confirm your phone number and email with the school office, and set the school app (ParentSquare, Remind, ClassDojo or your district's app) to deliver urgent alerts instantly even if everything else is a digest.
Update pickup permissions and emergency contacts before substitutes and holiday schedules kick in.
Giving Tuesday is the Tuesday after US Thanksgiving (December 1 in 2026). If your PTA takes part, send the thank-you and the total raised in the first week of December.
Wrap up holiday food and coat drives: deliver to your partner organization before break, then share totals and thank volunteers.
Teacher and staff thank-yous: keep gifts optional and give families a no-cost option such as a handwritten note from the student.
Sweep the lost-and-found with your child before break, and return library books and borrowed devices if the school asks.
Winter clothes check: layers, a hat, mittens or gloves, and insulated boots, plus a dry change of clothes in the backpack for younger kids.
Gift check: follow CPSC toy safety basics before wrapping (see Holiday gift check: toy safety rules from CPSC)

New games or devices for the holidays: link a parent account and set chat and spending limits (see Roblox parental controls: link your account and set chat, spending and screen time)

Game console under the tree? Set play time, bedtime and spending limits before it's wrapped (see Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 parental controls: set them up before the holidays)
New tablet or phone? Set up YouTube supervision and a Shorts limit in Family Center (see YouTube for kids and teens: supervised accounts, YouTube Kids and Shorts limits)

pages.title: Daylight saving time ends Nov 1: help your kids' sleep adjust
pages.seoTitle: Fall back Nov 1, 2026: a kids' sleep plan for parents
pages.summary: Clocks fall back one hour at 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 1, 2026. Ease kids in by moving bedtime, wake time and meals 15–20 minutes later for a few nights beforehand, keep early mornings dim until wake-up time, and hold the bedtime routine steady. Most kids settle within a week or two.
steps: Put "Clocks fall back: Sun Nov 1, 2 a.m." on the family calendar. Hawaii and most of Arizona don't change their clocks.

For a few nights before (from about Wed Oct 28), move bedtime, wake time and dinner 15–20 minutes later each night. For little ones, the AAP suggests nudging naps and bedtime a few minutes a day starting about a week ahead.
Teen already short on sleep? Skip the later shift and let them use the extra hour. The AASM says people with chronic sleep loss benefit from that "extra" hour.
Saturday evening, set the clocks back and go to bed at your normal bedtime.
For early risers, keep the room dark and lights low until the new wake-up time, then get outside in daylight during the day.
Screens away at least an hour before bed, and charge phones outside the bedroom.
Keep the same short bedtime routine every night. If sleep is still off after about two weeks, talk with your pediatrician.

ul: Ages 3–5: 10–13 hours per 24 hours, including naps
Ages 6–12: 9–12 hours a night
Teens 13–18: 8–10 hours a night

blocks.h: Why the fall change still disrupts kids
p: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia notes that for kids a 7 a.m. wake-up feels like 8 a.m. after the change and an 8 p.m. bedtime feels like 9 p.m., so young early birds may wake earlier and crash before bedtime. CHOP says a consistent routine usually gets kids adjusted within a week or two, and the AAP says kids usually adjust within about a week.
Add a one-line reminder about the time change to your last October newsletter or school-app post, and remind families the bus and bell times don't change even though the clocks do.

pages.seoTitle: Sick day or school day? AAP and CDC guidance for parents
pages.summary: As a general rule, the AAP says to keep kids home if they've had a fever above 101°F in the past 24 hours, vomiting or diarrhea in the past 24 hours, or aren't well enough to take part in class. CDC school guidance says they can usually return once they've had no fever for 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine and are getting better overall. Your school's policy comes first.
steps: Find your school's illness policy now, in the handbook or on the nurse's page. Fever cutoffs and return rules vary by district, so use your school's numbers when they differ.
On a sick morning, ask three questions: Fever above 101°F in the past 24 hours? Vomiting or diarrhea in the past 24 hours? Well enough to join in class? A yes to any of them means a home day.

Just a leftover runny nose or a slight headache? The AAP says that, depending on local attendance policy, kids can go to school if none of the three apply. Make sure the school can reach you during the day.
Going back: wait until there's been no fever for at least 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine and symptoms are getting better overall.
Report the absence the way your school asks (attendance line, app or email) and ask how to get any missed work.
Line up a backup caregiver before cold and flu season peaks.
Call your pediatrician with questions. For emergency warning signs such as trouble breathing or chest pain, get emergency care right away.

ul: Stay home with: a fever (including a fever with a new rash); vomiting more than twice in the past 24 hours; diarrhea that causes accidents, is bloody, or means more than two extra bowel movements in 24 hours; draining skin sores that can't be covered; or respiratory symptoms that are getting worse or not improving.
In general, CDC says children with improving symptoms should be able to take part in school.
CDC also asks schools to think carefully before requiring a doctor's note for illness absences, since many common childhood illnesses can be managed at home.

p: Share a short version of your school's sick-day policy and how to report an absence in your November newsletter or school-app post. It saves the front office a lot of morning phone calls.

pages.seoTitle: Halloween safety checklist for parents: AAP and FDA tips
pages.summary: Halloween 2026 falls on a Saturday. The AAP's checklist: bright, well-fitting costumes with makeup instead of masks, an adult with young kids and a group plan for older ones, crosswalks and well-lit streets, and checking every treat at home before anyone eats it. Plan ahead for food allergies.
steps: Costumes: make sure costumes and shoes fit and are short enough not to trip on. Add reflective tape or glow sticks, look for "flame resistant" on labels, and consider face paint (patch-test it first) instead of a mask that blocks vision.
Skip decorative contact lenses unless an eye care professional has examined your child and written a prescription. The AAP notes they're a medical device.
Young kids: an adult goes along. Older kids: go in a group, agree on the route and a check-in time, and carry a flashlight.
Street rules: cross as a group at crosswalks, never between parked cars, stay on sidewalks and well-lit streets, and put phones away while walking.
Feed everyone a meal before heading out, so nobody snacks from the bag on the way.
At home, check every treat before eating. Throw out anything unwrapped, torn, discolored or with tiny pinholes. The FDA says not to eat anything that isn't commercially wrapped.
Little ones: remove choking hazards such as gum, peanuts, hard candy and small toys.
Food allergies: read every label, skip home-baked treats, and carry any prescribed epinephrine. Look for houses with a teal pumpkin, which signals non-food treats.

ul: Clear the porch and path of hoses, toys and wet leaves, check outdoor lights, and keep pets away from the door.
Use a flameless candle or flashlight in jack-o'-lanterns, and keep any lit pumpkin away from where visitors walk.
Offer a bowl of non-food treats (glow sticks, stickers, pencils) and add your address to FARE's Teal Pumpkin Project map so families managing food allergies can find you.

p: The AAP says child pedestrian injuries are more likely on Halloween than on any other night, and suggests clear rules for teens who drive: slow down in neighborhoods, especially near driveways, alleys and parked cars.

Share your school's costume policy for any daytime parade or class party, and remind families that home-baked treats can be a problem for classmates with food allergies. A teal pumpkin at a school trunk-or-treat is an easy way to include everyone.

pages.seoTitle: FAFSA 2027–28 for parents of seniors: deadlines and tips
pages.summary: The 2027–28 FAFSA opened September 23, 2026 and covers college or trade school from July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2028. The student and each parent who must add information need their own StudentAid.gov account. State and college deadlines come much earlier than the federal one, and some aid runs out.
steps: Create StudentAid.gov accounts now: one for your student and one for each parent who has to add information. Use StudentAid.gov's "Who needs a StudentAid.gov account" tool if you're not sure who that is. Each account needs a name exactly as it appears on the Social Security card, date of birth, email and Social Security number (if you have one).
Look up your state's deadline on StudentAid.gov's FAFSA deadlines page, plus each college's own deadline. Put the earliest one on the family calendar.
Expect the form to ask about 2025 taxes. The 2027–28 FAFSA uses tax information from two years before the award year, and most people can import federal tax information directly.

Have the other details handy: current balances of checking and savings accounts, cash over $1,000, child support received, and the value of any investments, businesses or farms (not counting retirement accounts).
Your student starts the form on the official .gov site and invites you as a contributor. Then you log in with your own account, add your section and sign.
List every college your student might attend, then check the FAFSA Submission Summary when it arrives. StudentAid.gov says most forms are processed immediately and some take one to three days.

ul: Federal: the 2027–28 FAFSA must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. Central time on June 30, 2028. That's far too late for most state and college aid.

States set their own deadlines, and some award aid until funds run out. For example, StudentAid.gov lists March 2, 2027 for most California state aid programs, and "as soon as possible after Oct. 1, 2026" for Illinois' Monetary Award Program.
Each college may set its own deadline and may define it differently (for example, the date your form is processed or the date the school receives your data). Ask each school.
The FAFSA is free. If a website asks you to pay to fill it out, you're on the wrong site. The real form is on a .gov website.
Keep your records, but don't mail them to Federal Student Aid.
If your student submitted during the early testing period and it went through, StudentAid.gov says they don't need to submit again.

p: High school PTSAs can add a one-line FAFSA reminder (with the state deadline) to the November newsletter, and ask the counseling office whether it's hosting a FAFSA help night.

pages.seoTitle: Holiday road trip car seat check: NHTSA guidelines by age
pages.summary: Before Thanksgiving travel (Thursday, Nov 26), check that each child is in the right seat for their size, that every seat is installed with either the seat belt or the lower anchors (never both) plus the top tether for forward-facing seats, and that kids under 13 ride in the back. Flying? The FAA says a child under 2 is safest in an approved car seat in their own airplane seat.
steps: Match the seat to the child (NHTSA): rear-facing until they reach the seat's top rear-facing height or weight limit, then forward-facing with a harness and tether, then a booster until the adult belt fits, and the back seat through at least age 12.

Belt-fit test for older kids: the lap belt lies snugly across the upper thighs, not the stomach, and the shoulder belt crosses the shoulder and chest, not the neck or face. If not, they still need a booster.
Installation: use the lower anchors or the vehicle seat belt, not both. For forward-facing seats, NHTSA recommends always using the top tether when the car seat and vehicle manufacturers allow it.
Check the lower-anchor weight limit on the car seat's label. NHTSA says that once your child outgrows it, reinstall the seat with the seat belt.
Riding in Grandma's car or a rental? Install the seat yourself before the trip and read both the car seat manual and the vehicle manual.
Unsure? NHTSA lists car seat inspection stations where certified technicians check seats, free of charge in most cases. Book early in November.
Register your seat with the manufacturer, or sign up for NHTSA recall alerts, so you hear about recalls.

ul: The FAA says the safest place for a child under 2 is in an approved child restraint in their own seat, not on a lap, and buying a ticket for your child is the only way to guarantee you can use one.
Look for the label "This restraint is certified for use in motor vehicles and aircraft."
Booster seats and backless child restraints can't be used on a plane during taxi, takeoff or landing. Check them as baggage.
Ask your airline about seating your family together; car seats generally go in a window seat and never in an exit row.

p: Add one line to the pre-Thanksgiving newsletter pointing families to NHTSA's car seat page and the nearest inspection station, and check whether your local fire department, police department or hospital runs a car seat check event before the holidays.

pages.summary: Schools send meal applications home at the start of the year, but USDA says families can apply for free or reduced-price school meals any time during the school year, straight to the school or district. Households that get SNAP, and some other benefits, often qualify automatically. Some schools already serve every student free meals.
steps: If your income dropped, you lost a job or your household grew, don't wait for next fall. Ask the school office or district nutrition department for a meal application, or find it on the district website.
Getting SNAP? USDA says all your children who attend school automatically qualify for free meals. TANF also gives automatic eligibility. Ask the school whether you still need to fill anything out.
Getting WIC or unemployment benefits? USDA says you may also be eligible, so ask the school.
Fill out one application per household if your district allows it, and list every child in the household who attends school there.
Check whether your school uses the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP). In CEP schools, every enrolled student gets breakfast and lunch at no cost and families don't fill out applications.
Watch for the approval letter, and keep paying or packing lunch until it arrives.

ul: Applications are reviewed by local school or district officials, who decide on free or reduced-price benefits.
Income limits are set each year by USDA; your district's application lists the current numbers.
Meal applications are confidential. If you're worried about privacy, ask the district who sees your form.

p: Before Thanksgiving and winter break, add a short, no-judgment note to the newsletter: "Money tight this year? You can apply for free or reduced-price school meals any time. Ask the office." Pair it with your holiday food drive, and never ask families to tell the PTA whether they applied.

pages.seoTitle: Holiday toy safety checklist for parents (CPSC guidance)
pages.summary: Before wrapping gifts, check the age label, keep small parts away from kids under 3 and deflated balloons from kids under 8, look for screw-secured battery compartments on anything with button or coin batteries, skip water beads entirely, and add a helmet to any riding toy. Buy from trusted sellers and check used items for recalls.
steps: Read the age label and pick toys that fit the child's age and abilities. CPSC says toys that are a choking hazard for kids under 3 must carry an age label.
Keep small balls and toys with small parts away from children under 3, and deflated or broken balloons away from children under 8.

Anything with a button or coin battery (light-up toys, remotes, greeting cards, key fobs): make sure the battery compartment needs a screwdriver or tool to open. CPSC says a swallowed button battery can burn through a child's throat in as little as two hours.
Skip water beads. CPSC urges families to remove them from homes with children and urges schools and childcare to avoid them entirely.
Riding toys, scooters and new bikes: buy the helmet and safety gear at the same time, and make sure it's used every ride.
Buying online or secondhand? CPSC recommends buying from trusted sellers and checking CPSC.gov/Recalls for used items.
After gifts are opened, throw away plastic wrap and packaging right away.

ul: Suspect a swallowed button battery? Go to the emergency room right away and call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 800-498-8666 or Poison Help at 800-222-1222.
Suspect a swallowed water bead? CPSC says to seek medical treatment right away. Poison Help is 800-222-1222, 24 hours a day.
Report an unsafe toy or an injury on SaferProducts.gov.

p: Running a toy drive or classroom gift swap? Ask for new, unopened toys with age labels, say no water beads, and set aside any donated item with loose button batteries or small magnets. A one-line reminder in the December newsletter with a link to CPSC's toy page is enough.

Controls help, but they don't replace talking with your child about who they chat with and what to do if something feels wrong.

pages.title: Missing two days a month adds up: what parents should know about chronic absence
pages.seoTitle: Chronic absence explained for parents: 10% of school days
pages.summary: Chronic absence means missing 10% or more of school days for any reason: excused, unexcused or suspensions. Attendance Works says that's about 18 days in most districts, or just two days a month. With fall colds, holiday travel and long weekends coming, now is a good time to check your child's attendance and plan ahead.
steps: Look up your child's attendance so far this year in the school's parent portal or on the report card, and count excused and unexcused days together.
Do the math: two days a month by November is already on the path to chronic absence.
Plan holiday travel around the school calendar so trips don't add extra missed days before or after breaks.
Keep kids home when they're truly sick (see the sick-day guide), and send them back as soon as the school's return rules allow.

If absences are adding up because of health problems, transportation, anxiety or something else, talk with the teacher, school counselor or nurse early. Attendance Works says many absences are tied to barriers like these, not to not caring.
Ask what the school offers: make-up work, bus or walking-route help, health services, or an attendance plan.

ul: Chronic absence is missing 10% or more of school days due to absence for any reason, including excused absences, unexcused absences and suspensions.
Attendance Works says missing 10% of school, or about 18 days in most districts, hurts a student's academic performance. That's just two days a month.

It says chronic absence can make it harder to learn to read by third grade, achieve in middle school and graduate from high school, and that by 6th grade it becomes a leading indicator that a student will drop out of high school.
Federal data for the 2020-21 school year showed at least 14.7 million students nationwide were chronically absent, almost double the pre-COVID number of more than 8 million.
The federal Every Student Succeeds Act requires districts and states to collect and publicly report chronic absence data.

p: A friendly November newsletter note ("Every day counts: two days a month adds up") with the school's attendance contact and a reminder about holiday travel dates helps families without shaming anyone. Avoid singling out families or posting attendance lists.

pages.title: Your right to see your child's school records (FERPA), and how to fix a mistake
pages.seoTitle: FERPA for parents: see and correct your child's school records
pages.summary: Under FERPA, parents can ask to inspect and review their child's education records, and the school must allow it within 45 calendar days. If something is inaccurate or misleading, you can ask the school to correct it. Report card season is a good time to know these rights.
steps: Write to the school (principal or registrar) asking to inspect and review your child's education records. Put the date on it and keep a copy.
Under FERPA, the school must give you the chance to inspect and review the records within a reasonable time, and no more than 45 calendar days after your request.
Schools generally don't have to give copies unless something keeps you from inspecting in person (for example, you live too far away).
If you find a factual error, ask in writing for it to be corrected and explain why. The school must consider the request and tell you its decision.
If the school says no, it must tell you about your right to a hearing. If the record still isn't changed, you can add your own statement to the record.

Grades, evaluations and discipline decisions themselves usually can't be changed through FERPA. Ask the teacher or school about their review process instead. For IEP disagreements, use the IDEA dispute options.
Check your school's annual FERPA notice for its "directory information" list (such as name, photo and grade level) and how to opt out if you don't want it shared.

ul: FERPA rights belong to both custodial and noncustodial parents unless a court order, legally binding document or state law says otherwise.
When a student turns 18 or enters college at any age, the rights transfer from the parent to the student.
FERPA applies to schools that receive U.S. Department of Education funding. Most private and faith-based K-12 schools don't, so it generally doesn't apply to them.

p: PTAs don't get access to student records. If your PTA wants a family directory, ask families directly for permission to include their contact details, rather than asking the school for the list.

pages.seoTitle: Class holiday party food allergy checklist for room parents and PTAs
pages.summary: CDC says about 1 in 13 children has a food allergy, roughly two in every classroom, and that strict avoidance is the only way to prevent a reaction. Before the December class parties, room parents and PTAs can plan celebrations that every child can safely join, starting with non-food fun.
steps: Talk to the teacher and school nurse early. Ask what the school's food rules are and whether any students in the class have food allergies (without asking who).
Plan non-food fun first: crafts, games, a story, a dance party, or small non-food treats like stickers, pencils or bookmarks. FARE and CDC both recommend non-food celebrations and rewards.
If food is allowed, follow the school's approved list and let the teacher and families of students with allergies review it ahead of time. Only serve packaged items with full ingredient labels.
Keep allergens out of crafts and activities too: no peanut butter bird feeders, macaroni art or candy counting projects if they include allergens.
Build handwashing into the party, before and after any food. FARE notes hand sanitizer doesn't remove food allergens; soap and water or wipes do.
No sharing or trading food, and send home anything uneaten instead of passing it around.
Confirm the teacher knows where the student's emergency medicine is and that a trained adult is present, following the school's emergency plan.

ul: CDC: Food allergies affect about 1 in 13 children (8%) in the U.S., about two students per classroom. Strict avoidance of the food allergen is the only way to prevent a reaction.
CDC: Reactions can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis).
FDA: The nine major food allergens in the U.S. are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame became the 9th on January 1, 2023.
FARE recommends keeping classrooms food-free where possible, avoiding food in projects and rewards, and finding ways to celebrate that welcome every child.

p: Offer room parents a ready-made list of non-food party ideas and a simple sign-up for supplies instead of food. Never post or share which students have allergies; let the teacher and nurse handle that information.

pages.title: Freeze your child's credit for free: a parent's step-by-step guide
pages.seoTitle: How to freeze a child's credit (under 16) at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion
pages.summary: Kids usually don't have credit reports, so someone using a child's Social Security number can go unnoticed for years. Since September 2018, federal law lets parents freeze a child's credit for free if the child is under 16. The freeze lasts until you lift it, and the FTC says to request it at all three credit bureaus.
steps: Gather copies of your ID, proof of address, your child's birth certificate and your child's Social Security card. The FTC says the bureaus may ask for these.

Go to each bureau's minor freeze instructions (Equifax, Experian and TransUnion). Start from IdentityTheft.gov's credit bureau contacts page so you land on the real sites. The process for a child is different from an adult freeze, and you need to do all three.
Submit the request. If the bureau has no file on your child, CFPB and FTC say it will create a protected record just so it can be frozen. That record can't be used for credit.
Save each confirmation and the instructions for lifting the freeze in a safe place, with your child's other important papers.
Before you freeze, or if you're worried, ask each bureau for a manual search to see whether a credit report already exists under your child's Social Security number.
Lift the freeze when your child is older and ready to apply for credit, a job that checks credit, or an apartment. Teens who are 16 or 17 can request or remove a freeze themselves.

ul: FTC: If your child is under 16, you can request a free credit freeze, and it stays in place until you tell the credit bureaus to remove it.
FTC: Generally, a child under 18 won't have a credit report. If one exists, someone may be using your child's information.

FTC warning signs include bills or collection calls for accounts you didn't open, an IRS letter about your child's unpaid taxes, or being denied benefits because someone else is using your child's number.
CFPB: Freezing and unfreezing is free at the three nationwide credit reporting companies, and a freeze doesn't affect credit scores.
If your child's identity was misused, the FTC says to contact the companies involved, tell the three bureaus, freeze the credit and report it at IdentityTheft.gov.

p: A short newsletter note pointing families to the FTC's child identity theft page is a low-effort, high-value share, especially around the holidays, when families fill out a lot of forms. The FTC also suggests that when a school or program asks for a child's Social Security number, parents ask why it's needed, how it'll be protected, and whether another identifier or just the last four digits will do. PTAs shouldn't collect Social Security numbers for sign-ups or fundraisers.

pages.seoTitle: ChatGPT parental controls: how to link a teen account (2026 steps)
pages.summary: If your teen uses ChatGPT, you can link your account to theirs and manage settings like quiet hours, voice mode, image generation and whether their chats are used to train models. You can't read their conversations, and either of you can unlink. Here's how to set it up in about 10 minutes, based on OpenAI's help pages.
steps: Talk with your teen first. Linking requires them to accept the invite, and OpenAI notifies the parent if a teen later unlinks.
On the web, open Settings from your profile menu, select Parental controls, then Add family member. Choose Use phone or Use email, enter your teen's details and select Send.
Your teen gets a text or email link to connect their account. Once they accept, select their name under Family members.
Set Quiet hours for times your teen can't use ChatGPT, for example school-night bedtimes. You can add more than one time block.

Review the other switches together: Reduce sensitive content (on by default), Voice Mode, Image generation, Reference saved memories, and Improve the model for everyone (whether their chats help train models).
Consider Study mode or Study hours if your teen uses ChatGPT for homework. OpenAI says study hours start new chats in study mode during the set times but don't block access.
Check that your safety notification contact details are right under Manage notifications.

ul: Linking does not give a parent access to the teen's conversations, chat history or real-time activity.
One parent can link with several teens, but each teen can link to only one parent or guardian at a time.
Your teen can see which settings are on but can't change settings you manage while the accounts are linked.

OpenAI says linked accounts get extra content safeguards, and that in limited, serious situations it may send the parent a safety notification. Notifications don't include chat transcripts and aren't real-time monitoring.
When ChatGPT identifies the account holder as 18 or older, parental controls are removed and both people are notified.

p: A parent tech night or a newsletter link to this guide pairs well with the new-device parental controls checklist. Point families to OpenAI's own help page for current steps, and remind them that school-issued accounts and devices follow the district's rules, not home settings.

pages.seoTitle: Package delivery text scams: how families can spot them (USPS, UPS, FedEx)
pages.summary: With holiday orders arriving, many families get texts saying a package is delayed, needs a fee or needs updated shipping details. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service says USPS won't text you a link unless you signed up for tracking on that package, and the FCC says not to click links or call numbers in unexpected delivery notices. Here's a quick family check, including for teens with their own phones.
steps: Don't tap the link or reply, even to text STOP. Check the order on the store's site or app, or the carrier's official website, typed in yourself.

Look for the warning signs the FCC lists: pressure to act fast, a "redelivery" or customs fee, a request for card numbers, passwords or Social Security numbers, or payment only by gift card or crypto.

Report the text as junk in your messaging app, or forward it to 7726 (SPAM). For a fake USPS text, USPIS also asks you to email spam@uspis.gov with the copied message text (without clicking the link) and a screenshot.
If someone already entered information on the linked site, USPIS says to tell your bank or card company. Change any password that was typed in.
Talk to your kids, especially teens who order things or share a family account. Agree on a simple rule: no tapping delivery links; ask a parent or check the store app instead.
If an unexpected package with a QR code arrives addressed to your child or you, don't scan it. The FCC notes these "brushing" packages can lead to fake sites.

ul: USPIS: USPS won't send texts or emails without a customer first requesting the service with a tracking number, and those messages won't contain a link.
USPIS: Smishing texts try to get account usernames and passwords, Social Security numbers, birth dates, card numbers or PINs.
FCC: Package delivery scams may come as texts, emails, voicemails or fake "missed delivery" door tags with a number to call. A 10-digit call-back number can be international and costly to call.
FCC: FedEx and UPS say they don't ask for payment or personal information through unsolicited texts and email.
FCC: Scammers now also send texts claiming a package is "stuck in customs" until a tariff is paid.

p: A short newsletter blurb or a slide at a parent tech night before the holidays is enough. Link to the USPIS and FCC pages, and remind families that the PTA will never ask for payment or personal details by text link. If your PTA sells spirit wear or ships items, tell families how real order updates will arrive (for example, only from your store platform's email).

pages.summary: If your child plays Roblox, the most useful thing you can do is link your own Roblox account to theirs. Roblox says a linked parent account lets you manage content, chat, spending and screen time from your own device and get emails about your child's activity. Here's how to set it up, what changes as your child gets older, and the settings worth checking before the holidays.
steps: Link your account: on your child's account go to Settings, then Parental Controls, then Add parent. You'll sign in or create your own Roblox account and verify you're an adult with a government ID or credit card.

No account of your own? Roblox's Parent mode lets you approve requests on your child's device (with a 6-digit PIN), but it's still rolling out and doesn't include real-time alerts such as spending notifications.
Check your child's birthday in Parental Controls. Roblox uses age to decide which games and chat features they get.
Content: set the content maturity level (Minimal, Mild, Moderate) and block any specific games you don't want.
Chat: choose who your child can chat with. Many chat options need your child to complete an age check, and Roblox says users who haven't done one can't chat at all.
Spending: set a monthly spending limit and turn on spending notifications. Note that the limit doesn't affect gift card redemption.
Screen time: set a daily limit in 15-minute steps, and turn on weekly activity update emails.
Play a game together and show your child how to block and report someone.

ul: Roblox Kids accounts (ages 5 to 8) have all chat turned off; a linked parent can allow in-game chat where available. Roblox Select accounts (9 to 15) can chat with users in their age group and trusted friends, depending on age and region. The full Roblox experience is for age-checked users 16 and older.
Age checks use either a government ID or facial age estimation. Parents with a linked account can correct their child's age once after the first check.
From age 13, the child manages their own screen time limits and blocking, and spending limits no longer apply, though parents can still get spending notifications.
For teens 16 and older, parents only see notification, spending notification and activity update settings.
Children under 13 need a parent's permission to add a trusted friend.
Spending limits can be set from 0 to 10,000 in your local currency, reset at the end of each calendar month and may not apply on some consoles.

p: Before winter break, many kids get new devices or gift cards for games. A short newsletter note linking to Roblox's parent help pages, plus our new-device parental controls guide, is enough. Keep it neutral: the PTA isn't endorsing or rating the game, just helping families find the settings.

Once it's on, a parent of a 13 to 15 year old approves any change that makes the account less protective, and can set a daily time limit and sleep mode hours. Here's how to set it up and what to check before winter break and new holiday devices.
steps: Agree on it together. Instagram supervision needs both the teen and the parent to accept: either one sends an invite and the other accepts it.
Check eligibility: the teen must be 13 to 17 and the parent over 18. Only one parent can supervise a teen's account.
Send the supervision invite from Instagram, or have your teen send it to you. Invites expire after 7 days.
No Instagram app? A parent can use instagram.com in a desktop or mobile browser. Make sure your teen's app is updated.
In Family Center, open your teen's account and decide whether you approve setting changes or let your teen change them without you.
Under Their time spent, open Manage time limits and set a daily limit. Choose whether your teen gets a reminder or is blocked when they reach it.

Revisit the settings together over winter break, when schedules change.

By default, Instagram reminds teens to close the app after 1 hour of use in a day, and reminds them to close it from 10 PM to 7 AM every day (sleep mode).
Parents can change the daily limit and sleep mode, and choose to remind or block. A blocked teen can request extra time for that day.
If a teen sends supervision invites to more than one person, the first to accept becomes the supervising parent. Parents and teens can't block each other while supervision is on.

pages.summary: A Nintendo Switch or Switch 2 is on a lot of holiday lists. Nintendo's free Parental Controls app lets you set daily play time and a bedtime alarm, restrict games by age rating, limit chat and get a monthly summary of play. Spending limits live in your Nintendo Account family group, not the app. Here's how to set both up, ideally before the box is wrapped.
steps: Create your own Nintendo Account (you must be 18 or older) and add your child to your family group. Children's accounts are set as supervised; an older child already in the group can be set as supervised.
Download Nintendo's free Parental Controls app on your phone and link it to the console by following the app's steps. Restrictions take effect once the console connects to the internet.

Set a daily Play-Time Limit (anywhere from no limit up to 6 hours, and it can vary by day) and, if you like, a bedtime alarm. Choose Suspend Play When Time's Up if you want the game to stop rather than just alert.
Pick a restriction level (Teen, Pre-Teen or Child presets, based on ESRB ratings) or customize it. Because most settings apply to the whole console, set them for your youngest player.
Decide on communication: you can restrict communicating with others, and use the allow list to let specific games through.
Set a PIN (4 to 8 digits) so you can add time or change settings, and don't share it.

On the Nintendo Account website, open Family group, choose your child's account and tick Spending Restrictions to block purchases, plus Age-Based Content Restrictions for the eShop. Click Save changes.
On Switch 2, if your child is under 16, decide which friends they may GameChat with. Nintendo requires a parent's involvement, and each video chat needs your approval.

ul: The Nintendo Switch Parental Controls app is free and works with both Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch. Two parents or guardians can take part through Shared Parental Controls.
Play-time limits can sound an alarm or suspend the software when time is up, and parents can add time with the PIN. Extensions of 5, 15 or 30 minutes or 1 hour are available.
A bedtime alarm can be set between 4:00 PM and 11:45 PM, with play allowed again the next morning between 6:00 and 9:00 AM. Whichever limit comes first applies.
Restriction presets: Teen restricts games rated for 17+, Pre-Teen restricts 13+, and Child restricts games rated E10+ and above, based on ESRB ratings.
Parents get a monthly summary of play activity.
GameChat on Nintendo Switch 2 requires a parent's involvement for players under 16, who can only chat with friends the parent approves, and each video chat needs parent approval.

Nintendo eShop purchase restrictions are set on the Nintendo Account website by a parent/guardian account in the family group: Spending Restrictions disables purchases and auto-renewal on Switch 2, Switch and the Nintendo Store, and Age-Based Content Restrictions limits what shows in the eShop by age.
Settings carry over with System Transfer when moving from a Switch to a Switch 2.

p: Consoles are a common holiday gift, and setting limits before the first play is easier than taking them away later. A short newsletter note linking to Nintendo's parental controls page and our new-device guide is enough. Keep it neutral: the PTA isn't recommending a console, just where the settings are.

pages.seoTitle: YouTube parental controls 2026: Kids vs supervised accounts
pages.summary: New tablets and phones mean a lot of YouTube over the holidays. YouTube gives families three choices: the separate YouTube Kids app, a supervised kid account for children under 13, and an optional supervised teen account that parent and teen link together. Each lets you pick a content level and manage screen time, including a daily limit on scrolling Shorts. Here's how to choose and set it up in Family Center.
steps: Pick the option that fits your child. YouTube Kids is a separate app with a smaller set of videos, where you can even handpick exactly what they watch. A supervised kid account (under 13) uses the main YouTube app with a content setting you choose. A supervised teen account is optional and lets you see channel activity and set limits.

For a child under 13 on your own device: sign in to the YouTube app, go to Settings > Family Center and choose Add a kid account. Your child doesn't need their own Google Account for this, though they do need one for YouTube Music.

For a child with their own device: create a Google Account for them first, then set up supervision from families.youtube.com, the Family Link app, or by signing in to YouTube on their device with their linked account and entering your password.
Choose a content setting: Older kids (generally 9+), Teens (generally 13+) or Older teens (generally 16+). Age-restricted videos stay unavailable to anyone under 18.
In Family Center, open your child's profile and go to Time management to set a daily Shorts feed limit and take-a-break or bedtime reminders.
For a teen: either of you can send an invitation in Family Center (Settings > Family Center > Invite a teen or Invite a parent). Both of you must agree, and either can turn supervision off later.

Talk with your teen about what you'll see: you get counts and channel info, such as uploads, live streams, comments and subscriptions, and email alerts when they post or go live, not their full watch history.

ul: YouTube Kids content settings are Preschool (4 and under), Younger (5 to 8) and Older (9 to 12), and parents can handpick the exact videos a child can watch.
Supervised kid accounts are parent-managed accounts for kids under 13 (or the relevant age where you live), with a parent-chosen content setting, and parents can block channels.
Teens with a supervised teen account are placed in a content setting by age, Teens for 13 to 15 and Older teens for 16 and 17, and only a linked parent can change it.
In Family Center, parents can set a daily Shorts feed limit. When it's reached, the Shorts feed is blocked for the rest of the day and the limit resets each morning.

Take-a-break and bedtime reminders can be set for supervised teens. The take-a-break timer resets if the teen closes the app, signs out, switches devices or pauses for more than 30 minutes, and doesn't run for offline videos or casting.

With a supervised teen account, parents can see the channels their teen owns or uploads to, and how many videos, live streams, comments and subscriptions they have. Email notifications are on by default and can be turned off.
Teen supervision needs both parent and teen to agree to link accounts, and either can turn it off at any time.

pages.summary: Fortnite is one of the games kids most often ask for over the holidays. Epic Games puts younger players in a limited "Cabined Account" until a parent gives consent, and lets parents set a 6-digit PIN that controls chat, friend requests, purchases and which experiences their child can play. Here's what's on by default and how to set it up before the new console or PC comes out of the box.
steps: Know the starting point. If your child is under 13 (or your country's age of digital consent), Epic makes their account a Cabined Account, with voice and text chat, real-money purchases and some other features off until you consent.
Watch for Epic's parental consent email. If it didn't arrive, your child can resend it from Request Parental Permission in their Epic account.

Set a 6-digit Parental Controls PIN, either at epicgames.com/account/parental-controls while signed in to your child's account, or in Fortnite under SET UP PARENTAL CONTROLS. Use a PIN your child doesn't know.
Choose chat settings: who your child can voice and text chat with, or turn chat off.
Turn on the PIN requirement for friend requests if you want to approve who they add.
Set the PIN requirement for Epic purchases. Console store and Steam purchases are controlled by that platform's own parental controls, so set those too.
Pick the Fortnite content rating your child can play. Experiences rated above it need the PIN.
Turn on playtime report emails if you want a simple view of how much they're playing.

ul: Cabined Accounts apply to players Epic determines are under 13, or under the age of digital consent in their country.

Until a parent consents, a Cabined Account has voice and text chat, real-money purchases, non-Epic games, personalized recommendations, marketing emails, Sign in with Epic and account linking, custom display names and SMS two-factor authentication turned off.
Parents manage controls with a 6-digit PIN, set on the Epic account's Parental Controls page or in Fortnite.
The PIN can be required to add friends and to make purchases through Epic. That purchase PIN doesn't cover console or Steam purchases, or spending V-Bucks a child already has.
Accounts for players under 13 have a daily spending limit set by Epic, which a parent can override with the PIN.
Fortnite experiences carry content ratings, and parents can limit play to a chosen rating, with the PIN needed for anything higher.
Parents can receive playtime reports by email.

pages.seoTitle: iPhone and iPad parental controls: Screen Time and Ask to Buy
pages.summary: A new iPhone or iPad is one of the most common holiday gifts for kids. Apple's parental controls live in Screen Time and work best when your child has their own Child Account in your Family Sharing group. Then you can approve app downloads and purchases with Ask to Buy, approve websites with Ask to Browse, and set limits, all from your own phone. Set it up before the box is opened.
steps: Set up Family Sharing on your own device if you haven't already.
Create a Child Account for your child, so they have their own Apple Account and aren't sharing yours or a sibling's. Add it to your Family Sharing group.
Update your devices. Apple's newest parental controls come with iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, and Apple has a guide to upgrading to them.
Make sure you (and any other parent or guardian) are in your child's contacts, so their approval requests can reach you.
Turn on Ask to Buy: on your iPhone or iPad, open Settings > Family > your child's name > Apps & Websites > Restrictions > Ask to Buy, then turn on Require Purchase Approval.

Choose website filtering: in the same Restrictions screen, tap Filtering under Websites and pick Limit Adult Websites, or Approved Websites Only to use Ask to Browse. Allow school websites ahead of time.
Review App Store settings and the rest of Screen Time, such as when your child can use the device and who they can communicate with.
If another adult should approve requests, the Family Sharing organizer can set them as a Parent/Guardian.

ul: Screen Time parental controls cover which apps and websites your child can access, who they communicate with and when they can use their device.
Apple says your child should have their own Apple Account in your Family Sharing group, not share an account with anyone else.

Ask to Buy and Ask to Browse are on by default for children under 13, and Limit Adult Websites is on by default for children under 18. In some places Ask to Buy is on by default and can't be turned off for children under 18.
With Ask to Buy, your child must ask before downloading or buying an app or making an in-app purchase, regardless of the app's age rating.
Ask to Buy doesn't send a request when a child redownloads their own purchase, installs an update or uses a redemption code, so gift cards can be spent without a request.
If you dismiss a request or don't approve it within 24 hours, your child has to ask again. Missed requests can be found in Messages.
Parents can approve requests from an iPhone, iPad, Mac or Apple Watch.

pages.summary: If an Android tablet, phone or Chromebook is under the tree, Google Family Link is the main way to supervise a child's Google Account on those devices. You can manage apps, Google Play content, screen time and Chrome filters from the Family Link app. Set it up before the gift is unwrapped, and know what Family Link does not cover.
steps: Install the Family Link app on your own phone or tablet (Android 6.0+, iPhone/iPad on a supported iOS version, or a Chromebook that supports Android apps). You can also manage some settings at familylink.google.com.
Create a Google Account for your child under 13 (or the age that applies where you live), or add supervision to their existing Google Account, following Google's Family Link setup flow.
On the child's Android device (6.0+) or Chromebook (Chrome OS 71+), make sure they are signed in with that supervised Google Account.
In Family Link, open your child, then Controls > Google Play. Set content filters for apps and games, movies, TV and books, and review purchase approval settings.
Open Screen time > Time limits. Turn on Daily limit, set a weekly schedule, and optionally set bedtime or downtime so the device locks when time is up.
Open Controls > Google Chrome and Web. Choose Allow all sites, Try to block explicit sites, or Only allow approved sites, and add any school sites you want on the approved list.
Review account privacy settings under Controls > Account settings, and decide whether your child can change activity controls themselves.
Test: try installing a restricted app, opening a blocked site, and hitting the daily limit so you know requests and locks work before December mornings get busy.

ul: Family Link can create a Google Account for a child under 13 (or the applicable age) or add supervision to an existing account.
Supervised devices for screen time and app management are Android (6.0+), Chromebooks on Chrome OS 71+, and compatible Fitbit devices for some features.
Parents can manage apps, Google Play maturity filters, screen time limits, location on Android or compatible Fitbit, and Chrome site filters.
When a daily limit locks the device, the child generally cannot use apps (except those you mark as unlimited) but can still make emergency calls on phones with a calling plan.
Incognito mode is turned off in Chrome when the child is signed in with a Family Link-managed account.
On Windows, Mac, Linux, iPhone and iPad, a child can sign out of Chrome or use another browser, and Family Link Chrome settings will not apply in those other profiles or browsers.
Family Link does not supervise iPhones, iPads, or computers other than Chromebooks.
Google Workspace for Education accounts cannot be managed by Family Link.
Family Link purchase approval settings only apply to purchases made through Google Play's billing system, not every app's own payment method.
Content restrictions do not remove restricted titles from every search result or direct link; Google notes filters are not perfect.

Use the PlayStation Family app for on-the-go approvals, set a console restriction passcode so settings cannot be changed, and keep the monthly spending limit at $0 unless you intentionally raise it.
steps: Create or sign in to your adult PlayStation account, then set up a family as the family manager (Account Management > Family Management, or Settings > Family and Parental Controls on PS5).
Add your child as a child family member (web, PS5, or PlayStation Family app) and complete parental controls during setup. Child members cannot be removed from a family later.
Install the PlayStation Family app on your phone so you can manage playtime, spending and communication away from the console.

On PS5: Settings > Family and Parental Controls > Family Management > select the child > set parental controls (restriction level or customize age levels for games/apps, Blu-ray/DVD, PS VR/PS VR2, web browsing).

Set Communication and User-Generated Content to Restrict if you want to block text/voice chat with other players, sharing UGC, viewing others’ UGC, and linking select third-party communication apps (pre-written in-game messages may still be allowed).

Turn on Ask to Buy so you approve downloads and purchases on the watch.
Choose features on the following screens (for example Location Services for Find My, Siri and Messages in iCloud), then choose shared contacts, set a Screen Time passcode and turn on Schooltime.

Afterward, adjust settings from the Apple Watch app on your iPhone: All Watches → your child’s watch under Family Watches. Keep your iPhone nearby for updates—Apple’s guide says the setup iPhone must be within normal Bluetooth range (about 33 feet) to manage settings and update software.

ul: Apple Watch For Your Kids was formerly called Family Setup. It lets a family member without their own iPhone make calls, send messages and share location from the watch (Apple Support article published October 27, 2026).

pages.seoTitle: Holiday gift card scams 2026: warning signs and how to report
pages.summary: Gift cards are a favorite payment method for scammers because, once the code is shared, the money is hard to trace or get back. A federal banking regulator, the OCC, warns that no legitimate business or government agency will ask you to pay with gift cards. That includes urgent texts that look like they come from a principal, coach or PTA leader asking volunteers to “grab a few gift cards” for teachers. Here is what to watch for, how to buy cards safely and where to report.
steps: Treat any request to pay with gift cards—or to buy cards and send photos of the codes—as a scam. That applies to fines, bills, tech support, a “family member in trouble,” and messages that seem to come from school or PTA leaders.
Verify through a known channel. If a message claims to be from the principal or PTA president, call or message them at the number in the school directory, not the number that texted you.
Buy cards from trusted retailers in person or directly online. Avoid third-party resale sites and unsolicited “discounted gift card” offers.
Before buying a card off a rack, check the packaging and the scratch-off area for tampering. Keep the receipt and card number.
Read the terms: expiration dates and fees. Register the card with the issuer if that’s offered.
If you already sent codes: contact the card issuer right away, give them the card number and receipt, and ask whether the balance can be frozen or refunded. Then report it.
Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (or call 1-877-FTC-HELP), file with the FBI’s IC3 for internet crimes, and tell your bank if you paid with a bank or credit card. Local police can take a report too.
For PTA gift-card thank-yous or raffles, use one documented purchasing process (treasurer approval, receipts) so volunteers know a sudden text request is never how it works.

ul: The OCC (a federal bank regulator) says scammers trick people into paying for services or fines with gift cards, or steal balances from legitimate cards, and that no legitimate business or government agency will ask for gift card payment.
OCC warning signs include tampered packaging or scratched-off codes, unsolicited offers of free or discounted gift cards, and prize promotions that ask for payment or personal information.
The OCC lists ReportFraud.ftc.gov and 1-877-FTC-HELP (1-877-382-4357), the FBI’s IC3, the card issuer, your bank, local police and the retailer or marketplace as places to report.
The FDIC notes gift cards are like cash, there is typically little recourse when a card is stolen or misused, and you should report quickly to the issuer and keep your receipt and card ID number.
Whether you get money back depends on the issuer and how fast you report; there is no guarantee.
This guide is general consumer information, not legal or financial advice.

p: Add one line to November and December newsletters: “The PTA and school staff will never text you asking to buy gift cards. If you get a message like that, verify using the directory number and report it.” Pair it with your fundraiser and teacher-gift plans so families know the real process.

pages.seoTitle: TikTok Family Pairing parental controls: 2026 parent setup guide
pages.summary: TikTok Family Pairing lets a parent or guardian link their account to a teen’s account and manage screen time, scheduled time away, Restricted Mode, keyword filters, comments, messages and privacy. TikTok also applies its own teen safeguards (ages 13–17), including a default daily screen-time limit and muted nighttime notifications. Set this up before holiday breaks, when teens often have more unstructured time on their phones.
steps: Confirm your child meets TikTok’s age rules. TikTok’s Guardian’s Guide describes teen accounts as ages 13–17, with extra safeguards for ages 13–15. TikTok is not for children under 13.
Create or sign in to your own TikTok account on your phone, and make sure your teen is signed in on theirs.

On your phone, open TikTok, tap Profile, then the Menu button, then Settings and privacy, then Family Pairing. Choose the parent or guardian option and follow the linking steps TikTok shows; your teen confirms the link on their device.

Set a daily screen-time limit. TikTok says that for teens 13–17 this limit is on by default at 60 minutes (one hour). Family Pairing lets you change it from your account, apply one limit across the teen’s devices, and give a one-time passcode if you choose to let them continue after the limit.
Schedule time away for homework, bedtime or family meals—days and times when TikTok is unavailable. Your teen can send you a request to keep using the app during that window.

Review notification muting. TikTok says nighttime notification muting is on by default from 9 p.m. to 8 a.m. for ages 13–15 and from 10 p.m. to 8 a.m. for ages 16–17, and that those defaults override a custom schedule that overlaps them.

Turn on Restricted Mode if you want to limit content that may not be appropriate, and add keyword or hashtag filters for the For You feed (TikTok says it checks the words you choose against the post description).

Check privacy and interactions: whether the account is private, whether it can be suggested to others, who can comment, who can see liked videos, and who can send direct messages. TikTok says direct messaging is only available to registered accounts 16 and older.
Turn on activity notifications (for example if the accounts become unlinked) and look at the screen-time dashboard TikTok provides for the last four weeks.

If your teen uses TikTok in a browser as well as the app, also use your phone’s family tools (Apple Screen Time or Google Family Link) as a backstop—TikTok’s Family Pairing article points parents to those system controls for mobile and web limits.

ul: Family Pairing lets a parent or guardian link accounts with a teen and manage content, privacy and well-being settings, including screen time, scheduled time away, keyword filters, comment controls, who can message the teen, following/follower/blocked lists (where available), and an overview of privacy settings.

TikTok’s Guardian’s Guide lists default teen safeguards: accounts private by default; daily screen time set to 60 minutes; push notifications disabled from 9 p.m. (ages 13–15) or 10 p.m. (ages 16–17); “Suggest your account to others” off by default; teens cannot host LIVE; extra limits for ages 13–15 (no direct messages, tighter comments, no downloads, content not eligible for For You if the creator is under 16).
When you set a screen-time limit with Family Pairing, the teen needs a one-time passcode from you to keep using TikTok after the limit.
Restricted Mode and daily screen-time limits, according to TikTok’s Family Pairing help article, prevent the teen from logging out or switching accounts in the TikTok app.
Menus, defaults and feature availability can vary by age, device, country and app version.
Family Pairing is not a substitute for conversation or for device-level limits. A teen who installs another app or uses a friend’s phone is outside these settings.
Some features listed in TikTok’s help pages (for example certain interaction lists or the STEM feed) are not available everywhere.
Direct messages, LIVE, and shopping features have their own age rules; check TikTok’s current help pages for your child’s age.
This guide is not legal advice and is not a safety guarantee.
