pages.seoTitle: Fake school-closure and weather-alert texts: how families can verify
pages.summary: Schools and public agencies do send weather and closure notices—and scammers send look-alike texts and emails with urgent links. CISA, last revised January 26, 2026, warns people to be wary of texts and social posts related to severe weather and to confirm guidance with trusted local officials. The FCC tells consumers not to reply to texts or tap links from numbers they do not recognize, and to call back using an official number if someone claims to be from a company or agency. Pause, then check the school’s real app, website or directory number.
steps: Treat an unexpected text about a school closure, delayed opening, early dismissal or weather emergency as unverified until you check a channel you already trust.

Do not tap the link, call the number inside the message, or reply YES/STOP/CONFIRM to an unknown sender. The FCC’s consumer guide says not to respond to texts or click links sent from numbers you do not recognize.

Verify on a channel you already use: the school or district website you type yourself, the official notification app you signed up for, or a phone number from the school directory or a prior trusted message—not a number that arrived in the suspicious text.
If the message claims to come from the district, principal, bus company or a government weather agency, use the same “hang up and call back on an official number” habit the FCC describes for calls.
Look at how your school normally writes: unexpected wording, a request for a login, a payment, a gift card, a “confirm your child’s pickup” form, or a shortened link are extra reasons to stop.
If you already tapped a link or shared information, change those passwords from a device you trust, tell the school office, contact your bank if you entered payment details, and report the message.

Report the text: forward it to 7726 (SPAM) if your mobile carrier supports that (the FCC says most carriers do—check with yours), file a complaint with the FCC, and report the scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Internet-related crimes can also be reported to the FBI’s IC3.
For PTA and school communications, remind families in writing how official closures are sent (which app, which number, which website) so a random text is easier to spot.

ul: CISA’s “Avoid Scams After Disaster Strikes” alert (original date October 8, 2024; last revised January 26, 2026) says fraudulent emails and social messages with disaster-related subject lines, attachments or links are common after major natural disasters, and to be wary of social media pleas, texts or door-to-door solicitations related to severe weather. Confirm guidance with trusted sources such as local officials, FEMA and Ready.gov.

The FCC’s “Stop Unwanted Robocalls and Texts” guide (last updated February 27, 2026) says scammers create a false sense of urgency; do not respond to texts or click links from numbers you do not recognize; if someone claims to be from a company or government agency, hang up and call back using an official number from a statement or their website; and most mobile carriers let you forward spam texts to 7726 (SPAM).

The same FCC guide notes that certain autodialed calls about school closings are a recognized category of informational calls to landlines, which is why a fake closure or weather message can look routine. Legitimate emergency notices still should match the channel your school already told you to trust.
You can file unwanted-text complaints with the FCC and report scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) takes internet crime reports.
This is general consumer information, not legal advice, and not a promise you will recover money or accounts.
Official school alert systems differ. Ask your school how it sends closures, and use that—not a text you were not expecting—as the source of truth.
Some real school messages also arrive as texts. The test is whether you can confirm the same notice on the school’s known website, app or directory number.

p: Add one line to late-fall and winter newsletters: “The school and PTA will not text a surprise link for closures or weather pickup changes. Check the district site or app, or call the number in the directory.” Publish (or ask the school to publish) the exact official channels so families have something to compare a text against.

pages.title: Surprise app or game charges on your card: how to ask Apple or Google Play for a refund
pages.seoTitle: Kid made in-app purchases? Apple and Google Play refund steps
pages.summary: A new tablet or phone plus a saved card can mean surprise game and in-app charges. Apple lets you request refunds at reportaproblem.apple.com, and a Family Sharing organizer can see purchases charged to the shared payment method. Google Play says refunds for apps and in-app purchases may be possible within 48 hours; after that, you contact the app developer. Act fast, then turn on purchase approvals so it does not happen again.
steps: Find the charge. Search your email for the receipt (Apple suggests searching for “receipt from Apple” or “invoice from Apple”) or open Google Play’s order history, and note which account made the purchase.

Apple: sign in to reportaproblem.apple.com, tap “I’d like to,” choose “Request a refund,” pick the reason and the item, and submit. If you are the Family Sharing organizer, use the account button and choose All to see purchases charged to the shared payment method. If the charge was made on another Apple Account, sign in with that account instead.
Apple says to wait 24 to 48 hours for an update on the request, and that approved refunds can take longer to reach your payment method. Pending charges cannot be refunded until a receipt arrives.

Google Play: request a refund as soon as you can. Google says that within 48 hours of an app, game or in-app purchase you may be able to get a refund; you can also go to play.google.com → your profile picture → Payments & subscriptions → Budget & order history → Report a problem, and note that you would like a refund.

If a family member made the purchase with your Google account, Google says to request a refund rather than reporting it as unauthorized. Report unauthorized charges (ones nobody you know made) within 120 days.

After 48 hours on Google Play, or when an in-app item did not arrive or does not work, contact the app’s developer—Google says the developer can process refunds under its own policies and the law. Google says a decision usually comes within a day and can take up to four days; sending repeat requests does not speed it up.
Cancel any subscription your child started so it does not renew (Apple: Cancel a subscription; Google Play: Payments & subscriptions).

Prevent the next one: turn on Ask to Buy for children in Apple Family Sharing, and in Google Play require authentication for purchases (and purchase approvals through Family Link for supervised kids). Consider removing the saved card from a child’s device or using a gift card balance instead.

ul: Apple: some purchases from the App Store, iTunes Store, Apple Books and other Apple services might be eligible for a refund, requested at reportaproblem.apple.com. Refund eligibility can vary by country or region (Apple Support article published September 17, 2026).
Apple: if a receipt is for a member of your Family Sharing group and you are the family organizer, you can still request the refund on reportaproblem.apple.com.

Google Play: Google does not give refunds for most Play purchases, with exceptions. For apps, games and in-app purchases (including subscriptions), within 48 hours you may be able to get a refund depending on the purchase; after 48 hours, contact the developer.

Google Play: if you give your account or payment details to someone else, appear to abuse the policies, or do not protect your account with authentication, Google says it usually cannot issue a refund—which is why purchase authentication matters.
Google Play: if you buy multiple items in one purchase, you can only refund the entire purchase, and a refunded item is no longer available.
A refund is never guaranteed; Apple and Google decide each request, and rules differ by country.
Consoles and PC game stores (PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo, Epic, Roblox) have their own refund rules; check that company’s help pages.
This is general consumer information, not legal or financial advice. If you believe your card was used by someone you do not know, contact your bank as well.

p: A short December newsletter line helps: “Got a new tablet or phone for the holidays? Turn on purchase approvals before you hand it over, and if surprise app charges show up, request a refund right away—Google Play’s easiest window is 48 hours.” Link families to the Apple and Google help pages below.

pages.title: Winter concert and class party photos: what FERPA covers and how to opt out
pages.seoTitle: School concert photos and FERPA: what parents should know
pages.summary: Winter concerts and class parties mean lots of photos. Under FERPA, a photo you take as a parent is not a school “education record,” because the school does not keep it. Photos the school keeps can be education records when they focus on a specific student, and schools often treat photos from public events like concerts as “directory information” or ask for consent before sharing. If you do not want the school or PTA sharing your child’s photo, use your school’s directory-information opt-out—and ask before posting other families’ kids.
steps: Find your district’s annual FERPA notice (often in the start-of-year packet, handbook or district website). Look for the list of what the school designates as directory information—photographs are commonly on it—and the deadline and method to opt out.

If you do not want your child’s photo shared in newsletters, yearbooks, websites or social media, submit the opt-out in writing the way the notice describes and keep a copy. Ask the office whether the opt-out also covers PTA-run pages.
Before concerts and parties, check the school’s own photo rules. Some schools ask families not to post other children; follow those even if FERPA itself does not cover your personal photos.
When you post, crop or blur other children, skip names and school identifiers on public posts, and ask the other parent before tagging or sharing a close-up of their child.

PTA volunteers taking photos for the PTA or school: get the list of students whose families opted out, and keep those children out of anything you publish. Store photos in the PTA’s account, not personal phones, and delete what you do not use.
If you want to see a school-kept photo or video that focuses on your child (for example one used in a discipline matter), you can ask to inspect it under FERPA; see our school-records guide.

ul: A photo or video of a student is an education record when it is directly related to a student and maintained by the school (or someone acting for it). Factors include whether it is used for discipline or other official purposes, or whether a specific student is the intended focus (for example an ID photo or a recorded student presentation).

A photo should not be considered directly related to a student if the student is incidental or in the background, or is shown participating in school activities open to the public without a specific focus on that student.

Schools often designate photos or videos of students at public events (such as sporting events, concerts and theater performances) as directory information and/or obtain consent from parents to publicly disclose them.
A photo taken by a parent at a school event is not an education record, because the school is not maintaining it—unless a copy is given to the school and kept, for example, in a discipline file.

Directory information can include a student’s photograph. A school may disclose directory information without consent only after giving public notice of what it designates and how and when parents can opt out.
FERPA covers schools that receive U.S. Department of Education funds; many private schools are not covered. A PTA is a separate organization, so ask how your school’s rules apply to PTA pages.
State laws and district policies can add rules about student photos. Your district’s notice and policy are the source of truth.
This is general information, not legal advice.

p: Before the winter concert, post one line: “Please enjoy taking photos of your own child. If you share online, crop out other students or ask their family first. Families who opted out of directory information will not appear in PTA posts.” Ask the school office for the current opt-out list before you publish event photos.
U.S. Department of Education, Student Privacy Policy Office: FAQs on Photos and Videos under FERPA — https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/faq/faqs-photos-and-videos-under-ferpa

U.S. Department of Education: A Parent Guide to the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) — https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/resources/parent-guide-family-educational-rights-and-privacy-act-ferpa
U.S. Department of Education: Model Notice for Directory Information — https://studentprivacy.ed.gov/resources/model-notice-directory-information

faq.q: Can the school stop me from posting my own photos of the concert?
faq.a: FERPA does not cover photos a parent takes and keeps, but schools can set their own event rules. Follow your school’s photo policy, and ask before posting close-ups of other people’s children.

faq.q: How do I keep my child out of school and PTA photos?
faq.a: Use your district’s directory-information opt-out from its annual FERPA notice, in writing, and ask the office whether PTA pages honor the same list.
